paragraphs: It is a mitzvah for a person to be among the first ten in the synagogue, and the main point of the mitzvah is that he remain there to pray — not like those who are among the first ten in the synagogue and then go to pray in another synagogue, where they are not among the first ten, as mentioned in Sha'ar HaKavanot of our teacher [the Ari], of blessed memory. And just as it is a mitzvah to be among the first ten at Shacharit, so too it is a mitzvah at Minchah and Ma'ariv, and whoever comes earlier is closer to holiness and his reward is greater. And just as it is a mitzvah to be among the first ten, so too it is a mitzvah to remain until ten no longer remain in the synagogue; all the more so one must be careful not to be the first to leave among the last ten, for the first of the last ten who leaves the synagogue is the primary cause of the removal of the light of the Shechinah from the synagogue. See Eliyahu Rabbah, siman 93, ot 1, and Chesed LaAlafim there, and other later authorities.

clarification.explanation: It is a mitzvah for a person to be among the first ten who arrive at the synagogue, but the essence of the mitzvah is that he also remain there to pray — not like one who arrives early only to be counted among the first ten and then goes to pray at a different synagogue, where he is no longer counted among the first ten. And just as there is a mitzvah in this regarding the morning prayer (Shacharit), so too there is a mitzvah regarding Minchah and Ma'ariv. And the earlier one arrives, the closer he draws to holiness, and the greater his reward. And just as there is a mitzvah to be among the first ten, so too there is a mitzvah to remain until only ten are left in the synagogue — and one must especially be careful not to be the first to leave from among the last ten who remain, for the first one of them to leave causes the removal of the light of the Shechinah from the synagogue.
takeaways: Try to arrive early at the synagogue and remain there to pray, not merely to be counted in the minyan and then leave.
Be careful not to be the first to leave when only ten worshippers remain at the end of the prayer.

paragraphs: It is a mitzvah to run when going to the synagogue, and likewise for any matter of mitzvah, but one should do so in a manner that onlookers will not mock him; rather he should walk like a man who is quick about his work. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the verse "A king is held captive in the tresses" (Song of Songs 7:6) that the Shechinah is bound with Israel in exile on account of the two runs that Abraham our father, peace be upon him, ran for the sake of a mitzvah, as it is written, "And Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah" and "And Abraham ran to the cattle" (Genesis 18:6–7). And they also said in the holy Zohar that when Israel run to perform a mitzvah, correspondingly the angels who are their advocates run and hasten to argue in their merit. However, one should run only until the entrance of the synagogue; but within the synagogue itself it is forbidden to run — rather one should walk with awe and fear, for it is the palace of the King of Glory, as mentioned in Chesed LeAlafim.

clarification.explanation: It is a mitzvah to hurry and walk briskly on the way to the synagogue, and likewise for any matter of mitzvah, but in a manner that onlookers will not mock him — that is, he should walk like someone hurrying to something important, not run in a laughable way. Our Sages expounded on the verse "A king is held captive in the tresses" that the Shechinah is bound with the people of Israel in exile in the merit of the two runs that Abraham our father ran for the sake of a mitzvah (hurrying to prepare for his guests, and running to the cattle). And so it is explained in the holy Zohar, that when Israel run to perform a mitzvah, correspondingly the angels who are their advocates hurry to argue in their merit. But this law of running applies only until the entrance of the synagogue — within the synagogue itself it is forbidden to run; rather one should walk with awe and fear, for the synagogue is like the palace of a king.
takeaways: Hurry and hasten on the way to the synagogue and to any mitzvah, but in a dignified manner that will not provoke mockery.
Within the synagogue itself — walk slowly, with awe and fear, and do not run.

paragraphs: One who enters the synagogue should be careful to pause briefly at the entrance before entering, and to show himself fearful, trembling, and awestruck at entering the palace of the King of the world. This matter is very beneficial for a person's perfection and for [spiritual] attainment, and this is the secret of the verse "and you shall fear My sanctuary" (Leviticus 19:30). This is also what is said in the Gemara regarding Achitofel, who taught David the king, peace be upon him, the verse "We walked to the house of God with tumult" (Psalms 55:15) — that this also alludes to the matter of tumult, that a person should be stirred and awestruck upon entering the house of God, which is the synagogue — thus far the language of our teacher [the Ari], of blessed memory, in Sha'ar HaKavanot; see there. And in the handwritten book Keter Malchut it is written that every day, when one enters the synagogue, he should stand at the entrance and say the verse "But I, through the abundance of Your kindness, etc." (Psalms 5:8) and [then] enter; and as he enters and walks he should say, after the aforementioned verse, "The Lord of Hosts is with us, the God of Jacob is our stronghold, Selah" (ibid. 46:8), which is the verse of Abraham our father, peace be upon him; and after it the verse "Lord of Hosts, happy is the man who trusts in You" (ibid. 84:13), which is that of Isaac our father, peace be upon him; and after it the verse "Lord, save! Let the King answer us on the day we call," which is that of Jacob our father, peace be upon him. And if it is possible to say them all while standing at the entrance, how good that is; and if not, he should say these three verses as he enters and walks. And on a weekday he should not say the verse "But I, through the abundance of Your kindness" unless he is wearing tefillin; but on Shabbat and Yom Tov, when tefillin are not worn, he should say the verse "But I, through the abundance of Your kindness." And it is not necessary that he be wrapped in a [large] tallit with tzitzit — it suffices with the small tallit (tallit katan) that he is wearing.

clarification.explanation: One who enters the synagogue should pause briefly at the entrance before entering, and show himself fearful and trembling at entering the palace of the King of the world — and this greatly assists a person's spiritual perfection. This is the secret alluded to in the verse "and you shall fear My sanctuary," and likewise what our Sages related about Achitofel, who taught David the king from the verse "We walked to the house of God with tumult" — that one should be stirred and awestruck upon entering the synagogue. It is written in the book Keter Malchut that every day, when entering the synagogue, one should stand at the entrance and say the verse "But I, through the abundance of Your kindness, I will come into Your house" (only if he is wearing tefillin; but on Shabbat and Yom Tov, when there are no tefillin, he should say it always), and as he continues walking he should say three more verses — each belonging to one of the Patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. If it is possible to say them all while standing at the entrance — all the better; if not, he should say them while walking. There is no need to wrap oneself in a large tallit for this — the small tallit worn all day suffices.
takeaways: Pause for a moment at the entrance of the synagogue out of awe, before actually entering.
Say the special verses (of the Patriarchs) upon entering, according to the appropriate time and attire.

paragraphs: One should fix a place for his prayer and not change it — and not only with regard to his regular synagogue, but even within the synagogue where he is a regular he should fix a place there for himself. Likewise, when he prays at home from time to time, he should also fix a place to pray in each time. The primary requirement of fixing a place applies to the Amidah prayer.

clarification.explanation: One should establish for himself a fixed place for prayer and not change it. This applies not only to his regular synagogue, but also within that same synagogue — he should establish for himself a corner or particular spot. Likewise, if he sometimes prays at home, there too he should establish a fixed place for each time. The primary importance of establishing a fixed place applies especially to the Amidah prayer (the Shemoneh Esreh).
takeaways: Establish a fixed place for prayer for yourself and do not change it.
The main point is to establish a fixed place particularly for the Amidah prayer.

paragraphs: It is forbidden to pray in sadness, for if one prays in sadness, his soul cannot receive the supernal light that is drawn upon him at the time of prayer. Only at the time of confession (Vidui) should he feel sadness over his sins. And before prayer he should accept upon himself the mitzvah of "Love your fellow as yourself." Therefore, if there is a Jew in distress, he should pray for him explicitly every day, and through this his prayer becomes included among the prayers of all Israel and bears fruit above.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to pray out of sadness and gloom, for when a person is sad, his soul cannot absorb the supernal light that is drawn to him during prayer. The exception is the time of Vidui (confession of sins), when it is specifically fitting to feel sorrow over one's transgressions. Before prayer it is good to accept upon oneself the mitzvah of "Love your fellow as yourself," and therefore, if there is a Jew who is in distress, it is fitting to pray for him explicitly every day — and through this, one's personal prayer joins the collective prayers of all Israel and has a greater effect above.
takeaways: Pray out of joy and not out of sadness, except at the time of Vidui.
Before prayer, it is good to accept upon yourself love of Israel and to pray explicitly for someone who is in distress.

paragraphs: Even the Zemirot [Pesukei D'Zimrah] our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, would not say aloud, in order to show humility, and only on Shabbat would he raise his voice slightly, in a pleasant tune, more than his weekday custom, in honor of Shabbat. And when he would read some verse from the Tanach within the seated portion of the prayers, he would read it with its proper cantillation (te'amim). And he would warn our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, of blessed memory, not to put his finger inside his ears to clean them of dirt, from the beginning of the seated prayer until the conclusion of Aleinu L'Shabeach; however, [cleaning] by means of a handkerchief is not objectionable. It is written in the handwritten book Keter Malchut that when one says the three verses "Mi El Kamocha, etc.," which correspond to the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, one should count the thirteen with the fingers of the right hand, in the manner done when reciting the eleven spices of the incense — thus far. And he wrote well, for the counting expresses the importance and greatness of that matter, and since these are matters counted [in Scripture], it is certainly good to count them with the fingers to publicize their number, and this also helps to arouse concentration (kavanah) in the heart; and so I practice.

clarification.explanation: Our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, would not raise his voice even during the recitation of Pesukei D'Zimrah ("the Zemirot"), in order to show humility, and only on Shabbat would he raise his voice slightly in melody, in honor of Shabbat. When he read a verse from Tanach within the [seated portion of] prayer, he would read it with its cantillation marks. He would warn his disciple Rabbi Chaim Vital not to put his finger inside his ears to clean them, from the beginning of the seated prayer until the end of Aleinu L'Shabeach — but cleaning by means of a handkerchief is not a problem. It is written in the book Keter Malchut that when saying the three verses "Mi El Kamocha" (in which the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy are alluded to), it is good to count the Thirteen Attributes on the fingers of the right hand, in the way one counts the eleven spices of the incense. The reason: counting expresses the importance and stature of the matter, and it also helps arouse concentration in the heart.
takeaways: One should pray quietly and humbly, not loudly, aside from a certain raising of the voice on Shabbat.
It is good to count the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy on the fingers of the right hand while saying "Mi El Kamocha," in order to arouse concentration.

paragraphs: When he reaches the Shema recited before Parashat HaTamid, he should be careful to say the verses "Shema Yisrael" and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto L'Olam Va'ed" with great concentration, as with the Shema of [the blessings of] Yotzer — both with closing of his eyes, and with devoting his soul on the word "Echad" — for this is an obligation of rabbinic origin, and he should intend to fulfill the rabbinic mitzvah of Shema. There is great need for it in the rectification of the prayer, for we cannot complete the rectification accomplished in the Shema of Yotzer except by joining this Shema to it. However, it suffices to say the verse "Shema Yisrael" and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto L'Olam Va'ed," and one does not say "V'ahavta, etc.," as mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot. Now, in the prayer books it is written before this Shema, "Happy are we, that we rise early and stay late at synagogues and study halls, and unify Your Name every day, etc." But this is not an accurate text, for it appears to be a falsehood, since most people do not actually rise early and stay late at synagogues and study halls. Rather, the essential text is to add the letter kaf to the word she'anachnu and say "k'she'anachnu mashkimin u'ma'arivin" [when we rise early and stay late]. And it appears to me, the humble servant, that it is even better not to say "mashkimin u'ma'arivin b'vatei knesiyot u'vatei midrashot" at all, since before Heaven all is revealed, and what need do we have for such words? Rather, one should say "Happy are we, that we unify Your Name every day, etc." So it appears to me, and let the one who chooses, choose.

clarification.explanation: When one reaches the recitation of "Shema Yisrael" that precedes Parashat HaTamid (in the section of sacrifices), it should be said with great concentration, like the primary Shema recited in the blessings of Shema — with closing of the eyes and devotion of the soul on the word "Echad." This is a Shema of rabbinic origin, but it is greatly needed, since the rectification of the primary Shema (of the blessings of Yotzer) is incomplete without it. But here one says only the verse "Shema Yisrael..." and "Baruch Shem Kevod Malchuto L'Olam Va'ed," without continuing with "V'ahavta." Likewise, the text preceding this Shema should be corrected: the accepted text, "Happy are we, that we rise early and stay late at synagogues and study halls," is not accurate, because most people do not actually rise early and stay late at the synagogue. The essential text is to add the letter kaf and say "Happy are we, when we rise early and stay late at synagogues and study halls"; and in the opinion of the Ben Ish Chai, it is preferable to say only "Happy are we, that we unify Your Name every day," without the phrase about rising early and staying late — and let the one who chooses, choose.
takeaways: Say "Shema Yisrael... and Baruch Shem" with great concentration and devotion of soul, even though it is only a rabbinic obligation.

The essential text is to add the kaf and say "when we rise early and stay late"; and in the opinion of the Ben Ish Chai it is preferable to omit the phrase entirely and say only "we unify Your Name every day" — let the one who chooses, choose.

paragraphs: One should say Parashat HaTamid and the Ketoret [incense passage] with great concentration, for it has many virtues, since the reading stands in place of the [actual] offering. And he should count on his fingers the spices — the tzori, the tziporen, etc. And I wrote in my holy book Makbetzi'el, with the help of Heaven, that counting indicates importance and stature — for so we hold that anything counted [in Scripture], even among a thousand, is not nullified — and moreover, through this the concentration is aroused further. And there is a further reason for counting on the fingers: even though our reading stands in place of the [actual] burning of incense, nevertheless, because of the great preciousness and glory of this mitzvah, we join to the speech of our lips some movement of action; therefore we count on the fingers, to perform some action with our hands in this matter, so that speech and action are joined as if we had actually burned the incense. Therefore it appears to me that it is good to count specifically with the fingers of the right hand, and not, as some have written, to count with both hands in order to merit both hands equally — for one reason, the action of the right hand is more efficacious everywhere; and further, because the Kohen who burned the incense in the Temple would burn it with his right hand. And I further wrote there a reason for counting on the fingers: that the eleven spices are the rectification of the seven kings, which are the seven [lower] Sefirot: Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod, Malchut; and it is known that the five fingers correspond to Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, and Hod, as written in Sha'ar HaKavanot in the discourse on Tzitzit — so it is found that most of the seven Sefirot are alluded to in the fingers of the hand, therefore one counts with them. And in the handwritten book Keter Malchut it is stated that also the eleven spices alluded to in the verse "Take for yourself spices, etc." should be counted on the fingers, namely: for "Take for yourself spices" one counts two; for "nataf, ushechelet, v'chelbanah" one counts three more; for "samim" the second time one counts five more; and for "levonah zakah" one counts one more — and he wrote this well, and its reasoning is sound, and so I practice.

clarification.explanation: One should say Parashat HaTamid and the Ketoret with great concentration, for it has many virtues — the reading stands in place of the actual offering. When reciting the spices of the incense (the tzori, the tziporen, etc.), it is good to count them on the fingers. The reason: counting expresses the importance of the matter (following the principle that anything counted is never nullified even when among a thousand), and it also further arouses concentration. Furthermore, even though our reading stands in place of the actual burning of the incense, we nevertheless wish to join an actual action (the movement of the fingers) to the speech, as if we had truly burned the incense. One should count specifically with the right hand (and not with both hands, as others have written), because the action of the right hand is more effective everywhere, and also because the Kohen in the Temple would burn the incense with his right hand. There is also a further reason based on the Kabbalah: the eleven spices of the incense are the rectification of the seven Sefirot (Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod, Malchut), and the five fingers of the hand allude to five of the Sefirot (Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod), and therefore they are counted on the fingers. The book Keter Malchut also brings a way to count on the fingers the eleven spices alluded to in the verse: for "Take for yourself spices" one counts two; for "nataf, ushechelet, v'chelbanah" three more; for "samim" the second time, five more; and for "levonah zakah" one more — and so the Ben Ish Chai practiced in fact.
takeaways: Say Parashat HaKetoret with great concentration, and count the spices specifically on the fingers of the right hand.
The counting expresses importance, arouses concentration, and joins actual deed to speech.

paragraphs: Some are precise to say "Abaye hu havah mesader" [Abaye, he was the one who arranged (the order of incense)], adding the word "hu," so that the letter yud of "Abaye" will not attach itself to "havah," which would then appear as if one is pronouncing [God's] Name as it is written — and so it is fitting to do. And in the verses of Ana B'Choach, one should say every two words together — "Ana B'Choach" and pause; then "Gedulat Yeminecha" and pause; and so on in this manner — and one should have in mind the acrostics of the holy Names, as mentioned in the prayer books. And Minchat Aharon wrote in Klal 10, ot Kuf, as follows: and Shiyurei Kenesset HaGedolah wrote to stand while saying Ana B'Choach. But I have already written above that there is no obligation to stand except in a place where we are engaged with the first three [Sefirot]; if so, one should not stand when saying Ana B'Choach, for this matter is neither in Keter nor in Abba and Imma — thus far his words, and he wrote well. And I inquired about the custom of the Chassidim of Beit El, may they be remembered for life in the World to Come, and they said that it is not their custom to stand.

clarification.explanation: Some are precise to say "Abaye hu havah mesader" — adding the word "hu" — so that the yud of "Abaye" will not attach to "havah," which would then appear as if one is pronouncing the [Divine] Name as it is written — and so it is fitting to do. And in the verses of "Ana B'Choach," one should say every two words together and pause: "Ana B'Choach" — pause; "Gedulat Yeminecha" — pause; and so on in this manner, with intent on the acrostics of the holy Names (as found in the prayer books). Minchat Aharon writes that Shiyurei Kenesset HaGedolah wrote to stand while saying "Ana B'Choach"; but there is no obligation to stand except in a place where one is engaged with the first three Sefirot, and "Ana B'Choach" is neither in Keter nor in Abba and Imma — so there is no need to stand for it. And the Ben Ish Chai inquired about the custom of Beit El, and was told that it is not their custom to stand.
takeaways: One says "Abaye hu havah mesader" — with the word "hu" — so that the yud of "Abaye" will not attach to "havah" and appear as pronouncing the [Divine] Name as written.
"Ana B'Choach" — every two words together with a pause, with intent on the acrostics of the holy Names; there is no obligation to stand for it (and so is the custom of Beit El).

paragraphs: The Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael contains great secrets, and in the prayer book of our teacher the Rashash it is arranged properly; therefore one should say it calmly and deliberately. And in the handwritten book Keter Malchut, also regarding this Baraita, it is written: it is good to count the thirteen principles it contains on the fingers, with its reasoning given. And it is written in Sha'ar HaKavanot to say "v'chen" with a patach; see there. And some raise a difficulty: do we not find "ken" with a tzeirei in I Kings chapter 7 (verse 29), "and on the ledges was a base above," and further there (verse 31), "round, the work of a base" — all of this being from the same root as "He restored me to my base [kani]" (Genesis 41:13)? But this is not a difficulty at all, for indeed there is a "ken" with a tzeirei that carries this meaning, but "ken" with a patach is a clearer expression of this meaning. And it further appears certain that there is, according to the Kabbalah, a reason known to our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, why one must say "ken" with a patach.

clarification.explanation: The Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael (recited in the morning prayer) contains great secrets, and therefore one should recite it calmly and deliberately. Here too it is good to count on the fingers the Thirteen Principles by which the Torah is expounded. There is a grammatical discussion regarding the text: how should the word "ken" within the Baraita be vocalized — with a patach or a tzeirei? Some raised the difficulty that elsewhere in Scripture the word "ken" appears with a tzeirei in a similar sense, but it is explained that although indeed "ken" with a tzeirei exists with this meaning, nevertheless "ken" with a patach expresses the meaning more clearly, and moreover there is a reason for this according to the Kabbalah in the words of the Ari, of blessed memory.
takeaways: Recite the Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael slowly and with concentration; it is good to count the Thirteen Principles on the fingers.
Vocalize the word "ken" within the Baraita with a patach, not a tzeirei.

paragraphs: It is good, as much as possible, to join the recitation of the verses of Hodu directly to Parashat HaTamid and Eizehu Mekoman, without interruption, because in the morning Tamid offering they would say from "Hodu LaShem" until "U'vinvi'ei al tare'u," and in the afternoon Tamid offering they would say from "Shiru LaShem Kol HaAretz" until "V'Hallel LaShem." And according to the Kabbalah there is a reason for these verses, in order to separate the kelipot [husks of impurity] from holiness. And one who, for some reason, is unable to come early to the synagogue to begin the prayer from Parashat Ha'Akeidah together with the congregation, and is forced to begin alone at home until "HaShem Melech," should return and say the verses of Hodu a second time, in order to join them properly to the Zemirot according to the Kabbalah — for he was likewise obligated to say them at home, in order to join them to Parashat HaTamid and the other sacrifices. Now, it is known that the custom of the Ashkenazim is to say the verses of Hodu after Baruch SheAmar, while the custom of the Sephardim is before it, and both customs have a reason according to the Kabbalah. And it is known, as is written in Sefer HaKavanot, that our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, followed in this matter the custom of the Sephardim. And the verse "Hodu LaShem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo," which is within the aforementioned verses of Hodu, is not doubled — rather it is said only once. And likewise the Chassidim of Beit El, may they be remembered for life, do not have the custom of doubling it.

clarification.explanation: It is good, when possible, to join the recitation of the verses of "Hodu" directly to Parashat HaTamid and "Eizehu Mekoman" without a break, because in the Temple, at the morning Tamid offering they would say a certain passage of verses, and at the afternoon Tamid offering — a different passage. There is also a reason for this according to the Kabbalah: to separate the kelipot from holiness. One who is delayed and arrives at the synagogue after the congregation has already begun the prayer from Parashat Ha'Akeidah, and is forced to begin alone at home until "HaShem Melech," must go back and say the verses of "Hodu" again (a second time) in order to properly join them to the Zemirot, since he should have said them at home as well, to join them to Parashat HaTamid. There is a difference in custom: the Ashkenazim say the verses of "Hodu" after "Baruch SheAmar," while the Sephardim say them before it, and both customs have a reason according to the Kabbalah; but the Ari, of blessed memory, followed the Sephardic custom (before "Baruch SheAmar"). Likewise, the verse "Hodu LaShem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo," within the verses of "Hodu," should not be doubled — it is said only once, and this is also the practice in Beit El.
takeaways: Join the verses of "Hodu" to Parashat HaTamid as much as possible, without a break between them.
One who prayed alone at home and did not manage to join them properly should go back and say the verses of "Hodu" again with the congregation.
Do not double the verse "Hodu LaShem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo" — say it only once.

paragraphs: Master of the universe, may it be Your will before You to give us strength to arouse ourselves in Your honor, and to do Your will, and to arrange it all as is fitting. And even though we do not know how to set our intention and to come to rectify it all, may it be Your will that You be pleased with our words and our prayer, to bring about the rectification above as is fitting, and that the supernal chambers and supernal spirits enter chamber into chamber, and spirit into spirit, when they are joined together in their proper places, limb corresponding to limb, and they are perfected one with another, and united one with another until they become one, and they shine one upon another; and then the supernal soul of all, which comes from above, shines upon them, and all the lamps become illumined together as is fitting, until that supernal light is aroused, and all enters into the Holy of Holies, and is blessed and filled like a well whose waters flow and do not cease, and all become blessed above and below; and that which is not known and does not enter into reckoning, the will that is never grasped, hidden deep within them — that will is not known and cannot be grasped in knowledge; and then all becomes one single will unto the Infinite (Ein Sof), and all becomes complete from below and from within until it all becomes one, and the all is filled, and the all is perfected, and the all is illumined, and the all is made pleasant, as is fitting. Master of the universe, may Your will be with Your people Israel forever, and show the redemption of Your right hand to Your people in Your Holy Temple, and bring us of the goodness of Your light, and accept our prayer in mercy; may it be Your will that You support and sustain us, that we may speak words in a straight path, in the rectification above, in the rectifications of the Holy King and the Holy Matron, and to bring about complete union, to draw up that soul of all life from level to level until the end of all levels, so that that soul may be found within the vessel and spread within the vessel, for the upper and lower worlds depend on this soul and are sustained by it — thus far. And through this text, which a person recites every day before prayer, he will be spared from the curse that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai pronounced in the Idra Rabba, daf 141, amud beit (Chelek 3, 141b); and the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.

clarification.explanation: Before Parashat Ha'Akeidah one should recite the Aramaic text "Ribbono Shel Olam" ("Master of the Universe") found in the holy Zohar, in which a person asks the Holy One, blessed be He, for strength to arouse His honor and to do His will, and asks that the prayer help to rectify and unify the supernal worlds — that all the "chambers" and "spirits" join together properly, until they become fully united and the supernal light shines upon them, and everything ascends to the Holy of Holies and is blessed and filled like a wellspring that never ceases. Further in the text, one asks that God's will be with the people of Israel forever, that the redemption be revealed, that one's prayer be accepted in mercy, and that one merit to speak the words in a straight path, in accordance with the supernal rectification and complete union. One who recites this text every day before prayer is spared from the curse that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai pronounced in the Idra Rabba.
takeaways: It is good to say every day, before prayer, the text of "Ribbono Shel Olam" brought in the Zohar.
Reciting the text protects from the curse of Rashbi in the Idra Rabba, and assists supernal rectification.

paragraphs: I further found it written how good and pleasant it is for a person to say every day, after Tikkun Chatzot — that is, after saying the opening of "Eliyahu Zachur LaTov" — the words of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in the holy Zohar, Parashat Noach, daf 65, amud alef, and in Parashat Pekudei, daf 268, amud beit: Rabbi Shimon said, "I raised my hands in prayer above, for when the supernal will [is aroused] above, etc., etc.," until, "and therefore all stand — happy is the portion of the righteous in this world and in the World to Come." And if one was unable to say them after midnight, he should say them in the morning before prayer. And he should do likewise also on Shabbatot and Yamim Tovim, for these matters are exceedingly, exceedingly profound, and one who understands their secret will know how much benefit is achieved by reciting them for the rectification of that day, whether in the configuration (partzuf) of the days or in the configuration of the times.

clarification.explanation: I found it written that it is fitting to say every day, after Tikkun Chatzot (after reciting "Eliyahu Zachur LaTov"), a passage from the words of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in the holy Zohar (in Parashat Noach and Parashat Pekudei) beginning with "Arimit yedai b'tzalotin l'eila" ["I raised my hands in prayer above"], which describes how prayer performed out of supernal will has an effect above, and concludes with "happy is the portion of the righteous in this world and in the World to Come." One who did not manage to say it after midnight should say it in the morning before prayer. And one should do likewise also on Shabbatot and Yamim Tovim, for these matters are very profound, and one who understands their secret knows how much great benefit there is in reciting them for the rectification of that day.
takeaways: Say the passage "Arimit Yedai" from the Zohar after Tikkun Chatzot, or in the morning before prayer if one did not manage to.
Do likewise also on Shabbatot and Yamim Tovim, because of the depth of the secret of these matters.

paragraphs: A great and awesome matter, and a good and precious counsel, our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, revealed to us in Sha'ar Ruach HaKodesh, Yichud 21, and it is this: it is fitting for a person always to intend and regard himself as if he were a dwelling place and throne for the holy Atzilut [World of Emanation], and especially at the time when a person is praying, it is even more fitting and necessary that he have this intention, and through this a supernal holiness will rest and descend upon him.

And this is what he should intend: first he should think that he is preparing the skull of his head (which is the secret of Keter) to be a throne for the Name HaVaYaH vocalized entirely with a kamatz. And further he prepares the brain of Chochmah within it to be a throne for the Name HaVaYaH vocalized with a patach; and he prepares the brain of Binah within it to be a throne for the Name HaVaYaH vocalized with a tzeirei; and he prepares the right eye within it to be a throne for the five [instances of the Name] HaVaYaH vocalized with a tzeirei, which are the numerical value of "ayin" [eye]; and he prepares the left eye within it to be a throne for the five [instances of] HaVaYaH which are the numerical value of "ayin"; and he prepares the right ear within it to be a throne for the Name HaVaYaH spelled out thus: Yud, Hei, Vav, Hei-Hei, which is the numerical value of "ozen" [ear]; and he prepares the left ear within it to be a throne for the Name HaVaYaH spelled out thus: Yud, Hei, Vav, Hei-Hei, which is the numerical value of "ozen"; and he prepares the right nostril of the nose within it to be a throne for the Name HaVaYaH spelled out thus: Yud, Hei, Vav, Hei-Yud, which comes to the numerical value of "chotem" [nose]; and he prepares the left nostril of the nose within it to be a throne for the Name HaVaYaH spelled out thus: Yud, Hei, Vav, Hei-Yud, which comes to the numerical value of "chotem"; and he prepares the mouth within it to be a throne for the Name HaVaYaH spelled out thus: Yud, Hei, Vav, Hei-Yud, and the twenty-two letters of the five points of articulation of the mouth (which are the guttural letters alef-chet-hei-ayin, the velar letters gimel-yud-chaf-kuf, the dental letters dalet-tet-lamed-nun-tav, the sibilant letters zayin-samech-shin-resh-tzadi, and the labial letters bet-vav-mem-peh), which comes to the numerical total of "peh" [mouth]; and he prepares the right arm within it as a throne for the Name HaVaYaH vocalized with a segol; and he prepares the left arm within it as a throne for the Name HaVaYaH vocalized with a shva; and he prepares his body as a throne for the Name HaVaYaH vocalized with a cholam; and he prepares the right thigh within it as a throne for the Name HaVaYaH vocalized with a chirik; and he prepares the left thigh within it as a throne for the Name HaVaYaH vocalized with a kubutz; and he prepares the covenant [brit], which is Yesod, within it as a throne for the Name HaVaYaH vocalized with a shuruk with a vav; and he prepares the crown [atarah] within it to be a throne for the Name HaVaYaH unvocalized — thus far his words. And I found it written that when one intends this unvocalized Name of HaVaYaH, one must picture within the final letter Hei the Name Adonai — thus far his words, and this is a jewel of precision (kaftor vaferach).

clarification.explanation: The Ari, of blessed memory, revealed a great and sublime matter: it is fitting for a person, especially during prayer, to intend and regard himself as though his entire body were a "dwelling and throne" for the holy divine light (Atzilut), and through this a supernal holiness rests upon him. The detailed intention brought in Sha'ar Ruach HaKodesh is as follows: every part of the body — the skull, the brain of Chochmah, the brain of Binah, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils of the nose, the mouth, the two arms, the body itself, the two thighs, the covenant of circumcision, and the crown — becomes, through this intention, a "throne" for the Name HaVaYaH, with a particular vocalization or spelling suited to it (for example kamatz, patach, tzeirei, segol, shva, cholam, chirik, kubutz, shuruk, and so on), where each vocalization has a numerical value matching the name of that limb (for example, a certain vocalization equals in gematria the word "ozen" [ear], another equals "chotem" [nose], and so on). In other words, this is a complete map of the body, in which each part is devoted to a particular aspect of the Holy Name, like a precise "kaftor vaferach." And they further added: when one intends the Name HaVaYaH corresponding to the crown (which has no vocalization at all), one should picture in one's mind, within the final letter Hei, the Name Adonai — an additional detail in the secret of that intention.
takeaways: During prayer it is good to intend and picture the parts of the body as a "throne" for the holy Name of God, according to the intention of the Ari, of blessed memory.
One who wishes to practice this should first write out for himself the list of the Names and their vocalizations, and after becoming accustomed to it, will be able to intend them by heart.
In the intention for the crown (the unvocalized Name HaVaYaH), one should picture within the final letter Hei the Name Adonai.

paragraphs: And know that in the prayer book of our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory, further intentions were added to the order of the Merkavah mentioned above, to intend also with Da'at Elyon and Da'at Tachton; and further, in the preparation of the mouth he added to intend also with the Name Ehyeh. But I have recorded here only what is explicitly stated in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar Ruach HaKodesh. And what we have written here, any person can intend. First, he should write down the Names with their vocalizations in a book, and after he has practiced them, he will then be able to intend all of it by heart and will not need to look at what is written. Therefore it is good that he practice performing the aforementioned intentions every night on his bed, before he recites the Shema she'al hamitah [Shema upon retiring]. It is also proper to say afterward, seventeen (17) times, the verse "My eyes are always toward the Lord, for He shall bring my feet out of the net" (Psalms 25:15), and each time he should intend, with the Name HaVaYaH, one of the seventeen intentions mentioned — for the numerical value of these intentions corresponds to [the word] "tov" [good]; and one who reflects on the matter will find good.

clarification.explanation: In the prayer book of the Rashash (Rabbi Shalom Sharabi) further intentions were added to the order of the "Merkavah" mentioned in the previous halachah — an intention also in "Da'at Elyon" and "Da'at Tachton," and in the intention of the mouth they added to intend also with the Name "Ehyeh." Rabbi Yosef Chaim notes that he has brought here only what is explicitly stated in the words of the Ari himself, and that any person can intend this. At first it is worthwhile to write down for oneself the Names with their vocalization in writing, and after becoming accustomed to them, one will be able to intend it all by heart without needing to look at the list. It is good to practice these intentions every night on one's bed, before the Shema recited upon retiring. It is also good to say afterward the verse "My eyes are always toward the Lord, for He shall bring my feet out of the net" seventeen (17) times, intending each time with the Name HaVaYaH a different one of the seventeen intentions mentioned — since the number of the intentions equals [the numerical value of] "tov" [good].
takeaways: One may begin practicing the intentions of the "Merkavah" in writing, and later intend them by heart.
It is good to practice this every night on one's bed before the Shema recited upon retiring, and to say the verse "My eyes are always" seventeen times.
